primitives.name: Temporal Difference Encoder
primitives.verbatim_quote: A dynamic vision sensor observes a small, fastmoving ball, and a network of spiking Time-Difference Encoders deployed on the SpiNNaker neuromorphic platform jointly estimates its position, speed, and direction.
primitives.assumptions: Motion is locally linear; events are temporally correlated; receptive fields are stationary.
primitives.breakdown_regime: High-speed motion exceeding 10 m/s causes event overflow and tracking drift.

layer2.mapping: Maps event density gradients to velocity vectors using spatiotemporal correlation kernels derived from Hassenstein-Reichardt principles.
layer2.telemetry: Angular motion estimation error < 5 degrees, positional jitter < 2 pixels

primitives.name: Spiking Motion Estimator
primitives.verbatim_quote: The system achieves a hit rate of 56.1%, nearly double the human average, while reacting within 21.7 ms (with 5 ms network latency) and consuming an estimated 148 μW of dynamic power using fewer than 25 k neurons.
primitives.assumptions: System operates in real-time; neuron count is fixed; latency includes network propagation delay.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Latency exceeds 30 ms or neuron count surpasses 30k leads to performance degradation.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to a probabilistic graphical model where spiking activity encodes posterior distributions over motion states.
layer2.telemetry: Hit rate > 50%, latency < 25 ms, power consumption < 200 μW

primitives.name: Closed Loop Pinball Controller
primitives.verbatim_quote: Under more physically realistic flipper dynamics, the system is able to reproduce the full spectrum of human play styles, from cautious to aggressive, by tuning a single interpretable policy parameter, with no change to the perception pipeline.
primitives.assumptions: Policy parameter α maps directly to behavioral variance; perception pipeline remains invariant.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Policy parameter α outside [0,1] results in unstable or non-representative play styles.

layer2.mapping: Derives control actions from motion state estimates using a deterministic policy function parameterized by α.
layer2.telemetry: Style diversity index > 0.8, policy convergence within 100 steps

The core innovation lies in the integration of asynchronous event-based sensing with spiking neural networks to enable real-time motion estimation. Temporal Difference Encoders (TDEs) extract motion direction and speed from sparse event streams by leveraging spatiotemporal correlations akin to biological elementary motion detectors. This allows for efficient computation without redundant pixel processing. The spiking motion estimator then uses these encoded features to produce a kinematic state vector (x, y, v, φ), which is fed into a closed-loop controller. The controller's behavior is modulated by a single tunable parameter α, allowing adaptation to varying play styles. The system's reliability stems from its learning-free architecture, ensuring consistent performance under latency and energy constraints. Failure modes include event overflow during high-speed motion and loss of tracking when motion exceeds modeled dynamics.
